## Archiving and registering a reanalysis {#every-reanalysis-leaves-a-public-trail}

:::: {.none}
::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
**OSF**, the Open Science Framework: a public repository in which data, code and **registrations** are timestamped and citable.
:::

::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
A registration is a **frozen, dated snapshot of a plan**. Anyone can check what you said you would do, and when.
:::

::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
You need no account today. We read OSF the way that reviewers do.
:::
::::

::: notes
Outside a classroom, an analysis plan is preregistered by filing it in a public registry, and the Open Science Framework is the registry that most social scientists meet first. OSF does two jobs. It archives materials: the SCORE programme and Multi100 keep their records there, which is the only reason you can stand in the place of a real analyst at all. And it registers plans. A registration is a frozen, timestamped snapshot of what you intend to do, filed before you do it, which nobody, including you, can quietly edit afterwards. You do not need an account for any of this today. We read OSF the way a reviewer or a sceptical reader would, starting from the public record of the paper we have been working on.
:::

## The Multi100 preregistration {#the-study-you-are-inside-was-preregistered}

::: {.small}
- Multi100: **100 claims × at least 5 independent analysts**, no instructions on how to analyse
- The scoring rules – same conclusion? effect size close? – were **registered on the OSF in March 2022, before any result came back**
- Outcome: 74% same conclusion; 34% within ±0.05 *d*
:::

::: {.src}
@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness. Registrations: osf.io/dy68c (analysis plan) and osf.io/pzbqc (peer evaluation)
:::

::: notes
Multi100, the study in which you have been working as the sixth analyst, was itself preregistered. One hundred claims, five or more analysts each, and complete analytical freedom in the first task. The part that had to be pinned down in advance was the judging: what counts as the same conclusion, and how close is close for an effect size. Those rules were registered on the OSF in March 2022, before a single result came back, among them the rule that two results count as the same when their effect sizes lie within five hundredths of a Cohen's d of each other. That is why the seventy-four per cent and the thirty-four per cent that we met earlier mean something: nobody could move the goalposts once the results were in.
:::

## Preregistration templates {#two-templates-one-choice}

::: {.small}
- In your report: the **AsPredicted short form**, adapted for data you already hold – eight plain-language questions (on OSF: "Preregistration Template from AsPredicted.org")
- The fuller tool for a reanalysis: the **secondary-data template** (van den Akker et al. 2021, *Meta-Psychology*) – 26 items, built for analysing data you already hold
- Both templates are in your reading
:::

::: notes
There are two templates, and the course uses one of them. The preregistration block in your report follows the AsPredicted short form: eight questions in plain language, the shortest recognised template there is, and completable in about eight minutes. But it has limits. AsPredicted was written for people who have not collected their data yet, and its very first question, whether any data have been collected, has for us the awkward answer that we already hold everything. There is a template built for that situation: the secondary-data preregistration template by van den Akker and colleagues, twenty-six items, with a whole section on what you already know about the data. It is the tool that a full version of this exercise would use. Our block borrows that section and calls it the data-in-hand statement.
:::
